questions.text: What problem does the Projects feature solve for a teacher?

options.text: It keeps reference documents such as your curriculum and example lesson formats available to every conversation in that workspace, so the context does not have to be pasted in again.
It lets several teachers write into the same conversation at the same time.
It trains the model on your teaching materials so its answers improve over time.
It converts finished conversations into printable worksheets and slide decks.

questions.explanation: A project is a persistent workspace holding your reference documents, which solves the "fresh conversation" problem: every new conversation inside the project already has that context.

questions.text: Which of these does the lesson put forward as starter workflows for a teacher new to Claude?

options.text: Pasting in a long reading and asking, in one conversation, for a summary, comprehension questions at several levels of difficulty, and a writing prompt
Describing the topic, age group, available lesson time and objectives, then asking for a sequence of lessons to review and rearrange
Describing an assessment task and the performance levels you want distinguished, then asking for a rubric with criteria and indicators
Uploading a class list so that responses can be tailored to each named student
Sending a set of student essays and asking for final grades to be returned

questions.explanation: Processing a long reading, drafting a sequenced unit plan and drafting a rubric are three of the four recommended starter workflows; anything involving real, identifiable student material is ruled out by the privacy guidance in the same lesson.

questions.text: The lesson advises building genuine familiarity with a single AI assistant first, and only then trying a second one on the same tasks.
questions.explanation: The recommended approach is to work with one tool until you can routinely get useful results on three or four recurring teaching tasks, then run those same tasks through a second tool to see which suits which kind of work.

questions.text: How does the lesson characterise the practical difference between Claude and ChatGPT?

options.text: Claude often suits sustained, long-form work while ChatGPT often feels more like a quick-question tool — though this is offered as a generalisation, not a rule.
Claude is built on a different kind of technology and is not a language model.
Claude is designed for student use while ChatGPT is designed for teacher preparation.
Their outputs are effectively identical, so the choice comes down to interface preference alone.

questions.explanation: Both are built on the same category of technology, but their outputs differ noticeably on the same task — which is why the lesson rejects the myth that they are basically the same tool and suggests testing each on real work from your own week.
